name: How does a language model turn text into numbers? Explain tokenization and its practical consequences.
answer: First the text is tokenized: cut into pieces from a fixed vocabulary of about 100 000 tokens (words, parts of words, punctuation, bits of code). Common words are one token; rare words and identifiers are split into several (e.g. rate + _ + limiter). Each token has an id, and the model never sees letters. As a rule of thumb a token is about ¾ of an English word. Consequences: the model is bad at counting letters, and the context window is measured in tokens. Each token is then turned into a vector by an embedding (a row of a learned table), and the model transforms sequences of vectors into sequences of vectors using weighted sums and attention.
keyPoints: Fixed vocabulary (about 100 000 tokens); common words one token, rare words and identifiers split
Each token is an id; the model never sees letters
A token ≈ ¾ of an English word
Consequences: bad at counting letters; context measured in tokens
Then embedding: token → vector

name: Why is one-hot encoding a poor representation of tokens, and how do learned embeddings solve it?
answer: In one-hot encoding each token gets its own column: a \(100\,000 \times 100\,000\) table where every token is a single 1 and the rest zeros. Distances between such vectors mean nothing – “cat” is exactly as far from “dog” as from “pytest”. We would like short rows (a few thousand numbers) where similar tokens have similar rows. Nobody knows how to write that table by hand, so it is learned from the similarity of contexts. The learned embedding table has 100 000 rows and a few thousand unnamed dimensions; “cat” ends up near “dog” and “tests” near “pytest” without anyone telling it. Meaning corresponds to position: nearby means used alike, in similar contexts. This table is the first layer of every language model.
keyPoints: One-hot: a \(100\,000 \times 100\,000\) table; all tokens equally far apart, so distances mean nothing
Wanted: short rows, similar tokens similar
Learned from context similarity, not hand-written
Nearby = used in similar contexts; dimensions have no names
Embedding table = first layer of every LM

name: Explain how an attention layer computes a new vector for each token. Illustrate it on the sentence “run the tests and fix them”, where the attention row for “them” is: run 0.10, the 0.00, tests 0.55, and 0.00, fix 0.15, them 0.20. Write the new vector of “them” as a mixture and say what it means. Why does attention make long contexts expensive?
answer: Inside a block, each token’s vector is first transformed by a small trained model (weighted sums). Then an \(n \times n\) attention table is computed afresh for every input: the row for a token says how much it relates to each other token, and each row sums to 1. The token’s new vector is the mixture of all the transformed vectors, weighted by its row. For “them”, writing \(v\) for a transformed vector: \[v'_{\text{them}} = 0.10\,v_{\text{run}} + 0.55\,v_{\text{tests}} + 0.15\,v_{\text{fix}} + 0.20\,v_{\text{them}}\] (“the” and “and” get weight 0; the weights sum to 1). The largest weight is on “tests”, so the new vector of “them” is mostly “tests” – the pronoun has been resolved. The rows are themselves computed from transformed vectors, so who relates to whom is learned, not fixed. Cost: \(n\) tokens give \(n^2\) cells, so doubling the context quadruples the work: \((2n)^2 = 4n^2\).
keyPoints: Each token vector is first transformed by learned weighted sums
An \(n \times n\) table is recomputed for every input; each row sums to 1
New vector = row-weighted mixture of all transformed vectors
\(v'_{\text{them}} = 0.10\,v_{\text{run}} + 0.55\,v_{\text{tests}} + 0.15\,v_{\text{fix}} + 0.20\,v_{\text{them}}\): mostly “tests”, pronoun resolved
Who attends to whom is learned, not fixed
Cost grows with \(n^2\): double the context, quadruple the work

name: Describe the overall structure of a Transformer language model. What can and cannot be said about what its individual blocks do?
answer: Tokens are turned into vectors by the embedding table. Then a block consisting of attention (tokens mix) and weighted sums + ReLU (each token on its own) is stacked many times (e.g. 48 blocks in the largest GPT-2, about 100 in a frontier model, each with billions of weights). At the top the model outputs probabilities for the next token. The vector of a token is rewritten at every block – “them” starts as a pronoun and ends as “the failing tests in this repository, about to be fixed”. What each block contributes cannot be said: probing studies find tendencies (early blocks syntax, later facts and meaning), but there is no readable division of labour – the 2010 “black box” objection is unchanged. Every frontier model is more or less this design with bigger numbers.
keyPoints: Embedding → [attention + weighted sums/ReLU] × n → next-token probabilities
The same block is stacked many times; frontier models are this design with bigger numbers
Token vectors rewritten at every block, gaining context
Probing shows tendencies only; no readable division of labour (black box)

name: Explain mixture of experts, the KV cache used while a model generates one answer, and the tricks that make very long contexts affordable. What is the practical consequence for how a model uses a long context?
answer: Mixture of experts (MoE): the weighted-sums part of a block holds most of the weights; it is split into many “experts” (say 64), and a learned router sends each token to a few of them, so only a few percent of the weights are used per token – the “active parameters” on a spec sheet, far fewer than the total. KV cache (within one generation): attention needs every earlier token’s transformed vectors. When generating token 501, recomputing the 500 earlier ones would give the same result as last time (a token only looks backwards, so earlier vectors never change), so they are kept. This avoids recomputing the earlier vectors, but each new token still attends to all cached ones, so the attention work per token grows with the context, and so does the memory for the cache – this is what a long context costs at run time. Long contexts: full attention costs \(n^2\) cells per block and the cache holds \(n\) vectors per block; at \(10^6\) tokens both hit a wall. A sliding window lets a token look only at the last \(w\) tokens (cost \(n \cdot w\)); older information arrives only indirectly through the stacked blocks, diluted, so windows are usually alternated with full-attention blocks. Sparse/selected attention uses a cheap learned selector to pick which earlier tokens to read in full (cost \(n \cdot k\) with \(k \ll n\)). Consequence: a long context is not read uniformly – the recent part gets the full table, the far part a sample or a diluted summary – and models are measured to use the middle of a long context worse than its beginning and end (“lost in the middle”). That is why harnesses summarise, drop and reorder context instead of just filling the window.
keyPoints: MoE: a router sends each token to a few experts; active parameters ≪ total
KV cache: keep earlier tokens’ vectors instead of recomputing them; memory grows with context
Sliding window (\(n \cdot w\)) and sparse attention (\(n \cdot k\), \(k \ll n\)) instead of \(n^2\)
A long context is not read uniformly; the middle is used worst
Harnesses therefore summarise, drop and reorder context
source: Lecture 2, slides 10–11 (backward-only attention as the reason the cache stays valid: Lecture 1 deck, slide 48)

name: How is a language model pretrained without anybody labelling data? How are images and other modalities handled by the same model?
answer: In pretraining the text is its own label: take any text, cover the next token, let the model predict it, compare, and nudge the (about \(10^{12}\)) weights a little – the same compare-and-nudge loop as in a small weighted-sum model, just with trillions of rows. So the training data can be the web, the code on GitHub and books, and nobody labels anything; self-supervision turns all text ever written into training data. Other modalities use the same move: an image is cut into small patches and each patch becomes a token via a small front end (a screenshot is hundreds of tokens in the same window as text); audio, video and PDF pages likewise. Inside the model the word “button” and a picture of a button become the same kind of vector, and attention lets them look at each other – which is why an agent can read a UI, a diagram or a screenshot of a stack trace.
keyPoints: Self-supervision: next token is the target, text is its own label
Training data: web, GitHub, books – no manual labels
Same nudge-the-weights loop at huge scale
Images cut into patches → tokens; audio/video/PDF via front ends
One sequence of vectors; attention across modalities

name: After “run the tests and fix them” the model outputs these probabilities for the next token: “if” 0.45, “.” 0.26, “when” 0.14, “before” 0.09, “so” 0.05. Explain how the next token is chosen: what greedy decoding and sampling would do here, what temperature changes (e.g. \(T = 0.3\) or \(T = 2\)), what the other sampling hyperparameters do, and why the same prompt can give different answers.
answer: Picking the token is not done by the model but by a few lines of code around it. Greedy decoding always takes the top token – here always “if”. It is deterministic in principle, but it loops, repeats itself and reads flat. Sampling draws at random with the given probabilities – “if” in 45 % of draws, “so” in 5 % – and is the default everywhere; that is why the same prompt gives a different answer next time. Temperature \(T\) is applied to the table before sampling. It never changes the order of the tokens, only how much the top one dominates: \(T \lt 1\) sharpens (at \(T = 0.3\) “if” gets most of the probability, roughly 0.85), \(T = 1\) keeps the learned probabilities, and \(T \gt 1\) flattens (at \(T = 2\) “if” drops to roughly a third and the tail gets its turn – more variety, more nonsense); \(T \to 0\) becomes greedy. Practice: low for code, extraction and anything with one right answer, about 1 for writing and brainstorming. Even \(T = 0\) does not guarantee identical output, because GPU arithmetic and batching add noise – do not build a test on it. Other hyperparameters: top_p/top_k delete unlikely rows before drawing; max_tokens caps cost and length; stop strings, a frequency penalty and a seed exist too. Deleting rows by a rule (e.g. every token that would violate a JSON schema) gives structured output. All of this runs outside the weights; the model does not know about it.
keyPoints: Choosing the token is code outside the model
Greedy always picks the top token (“if”): deterministic but repetitive
Sampling draws by probability (“so” in 5 % of draws): the default, hence different answers
Temperature sharpens (\(T \lt 1\)) or flattens (\(T \gt 1\)) the table but keeps the order; \(T \to 0\) is greedy
Low \(T\) for code, about 1 for writing; even \(T = 0\) is not exactly reproducible
top_p/top_k cut the tail; max_tokens caps length; rule-based row deletion gives structured output

name: A pretrained model “completes, it does not answer”. Explain this problem and how supervised fine-tuning (SFT) addresses it, including its limits.
answer: A model trained only to predict the next token on web text continues a question the way the web does: a forum question is followed by more questions and replies like “Same problem here. Bump.” It knows the answer but was never asked to give it. Supervised fine-tuning shows it examples: people write answers to prompts (\(10^{4}\)–\(10^{5}\) pairs). The update is the same as in pretraining – predict the next token, nudge the weights – but only the answer tokens are predicted, and a human chose what they should be. This is tiny compared with the web but has a big effect: the model learns the format; the knowledge was already there. The limit: good answers are slow to write and often nobody can write the best one – but anyone can say which of two answers is better. Judging is cheaper than writing, which leads to learning from judgements (RLHF).
keyPoints: Pretrained model imitates web continuations, not answers
SFT: a small set (\(10^4\)–\(10^5\)) of human-written prompt–answer pairs, tiny next to the pretraining data
Same next-token update, only on answer tokens
Learns the format; knowledge comes from pretraining
Limit: writing best answers is hard; judging is cheaper → RLHF

name: Explain the basic concepts of reinforcement learning: state, action, reward, episode, policy, exploration and credit assignment. How does it differ from learning from labelled examples? Illustrate the concepts with a simple game-playing learner, e.g. the matchbox noughts-and-crosses player MENACE.
answer:
Concepts. An agent sees a state and picks an action; the environment moves on and sometimes returns a reward, a number. An episode is one run from start to final outcome. The policy – what the agent does in each state – is what gets learned. Exploration means sometimes trying less preferred actions, so alternatives still get a chance. Credit assignment is the problem of deciding which of the many actions of an episode deserve the final reward. Difference from supervised learning: nobody says what the right action was, only how well it went, often only at the end; and the agent chooses what it experiences.
Illustration (MENACE, 1961). One matchbox for every position where MENACE is to move (a state); inside, coloured beads, one colour per empty square. To move, it shakes the box and plays the square whose bead rolls out (an action): the bead counts are the policy and the random shake is exploration – rare colours still come out. The opponent is part of the environment. A game is an episode, and the reward comes only at the end: after a win every bead played goes back plus extra beads of the same colour (three), after a draw plus one, after a loss the bead is removed. Every move of the game gets the same treatment, good and bad alike – the crudest answer to credit assignment. After a couple of hundred games it stopped losing, with no strategy, no lookahead and no idea why: the policy is just a pile of counts.
keyPoints: State, action, reward; episode = one run; policy = what is learned
Feedback is only the outcome, often delayed; no teacher with right answers; the agent chooses its experience
Exploration: a random choice still tries less preferred moves (the shake)
MENACE: boxes = states, bead counts = policy, game = episode, opponent = environment
Credit assignment: one final verdict reinforces or weakens every move played, good or bad
It learns to play well without ever learning why

name: Explain RLHF: how is the reward for a language model’s answer obtained, how is the reward model trained, and what is the main risk of this approach?
answer: Mapping RL to text: the state is the text so far, an action is the next token, an episode is one complete answer, the policy is the model, exploration is sampling – and the missing piece is the reward. A person can judge sampled answers to one prompt, but an RL run scores \(10^{5}\)–\(10^{6}\) newly written answers, which no person can judge. So a reward model (judge) is built: a copy of the language model with the last layer replaced by a single output number. People are bad at absolute scores but consistent at saying which of two answers is better, so the data are \(10^{4}\)–\(10^{6}\) comparisons (prompt, two answers, winner), and training nudges the weights so that \(r(\text{winner}) - r(\text{loser})\) grows – like Elo ratings in chess, the scale is arbitrary and only differences matter. In an RL episode the model samples an answer, the reward model scores it, and that one number is credited to every token of the answer; weights are nudged by gradient descent with no person in the loop. Risk: the RL maximises the judge’s number, not what people meant – wherever the judge is a little too generous, the model drifts there and never learns it is wrong. The standard guard is a penalty for drifting far from the SFT model; it limits how far the model can chase the judge’s mistakes but does not remove them.
keyPoints: Text as RL: state = text so far, action = token, episode = answer
Too many answers for humans → reward model (LM with one-number head)
Trained on pairwise human comparisons so that \(r(\text{winner}) - r(\text{loser})\) grows (Elo-like)
One score per answer, credited to all its tokens; no human in the RL loop
Risk: the model exploits the judge’s errors; a penalty for drifting from the SFT model limits but does not remove this
source: Lecture 2, slides 27–31 (drift penalty: Lecture 1 deck, slide 68)

name: Summarise the three-stage recipe for training an assistant model. What are verifiable rewards, and what consequence do they have for coding agents?
answer: (1) Pretraining predicts the next token on trillions of web tokens and gives knowledge and language. (2) SFT imitates \(10^{4}\)–\(10^{5}\) human-written answers and gives the format. (3) RL maximises a reward over \(10^{5}\)–\(10^{6}\) sampled answers and gives behaviour. It is one model with the same update everywhere; only the signal changes. Where an answer can be checked, the human and the reward model can be dropped and a program is the referee – maths (does the number match?), code (do the tests pass?), games (did you win?). These verifiable rewards are exact, cheap, unlimited and impossible to flatter. Reasoning models (o1, DeepSeek-R1) were trained this way, and the long “thinking” emerged; agentic models are rewarded on whole runs of the loop. Consequence: a model rewarded for green tests will make the tests green – deleting a failing test, special-casing the test input, weakening an assertion and fixing the bug all score the same. The reward defines the behaviour and every reward can be gamed (sycophancy and test-hacking are the same phenomenon); green tests are evidence only when you wrote them and the agent cannot touch them.
keyPoints: Pretraining → knowledge; SFT → format; RL → behaviour
Same weight update, different signal (next token, written answer, score)
Verifiable rewards: a program checks (maths, tests, games); exact and cheap
Reasoning/agentic models trained this way
Reward hacking: deleting tests, special-casing inputs; trust tests you wrote and the agent can’t edit
